title: Climate Science
summary: Understand climate change: weather, climate and the greenhouse effect, the causes of warming, the evidence, impacts on Africa, mitigation and the carbon budget, and adaptation and action for communities and individuals.
audience: Students, teachers, farmers, community leaders and anyone who wants to understand climate change

lessons.title: Weather, climate and the greenhouse effect

body.p: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular time and place: today's rain, wind and temperature. Climate is the average pattern of weather over a long period, usually 30 years or more. A single hot day is weather; a region warming over decades is a change in climate.

Sunlight passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth's surface. The warm surface gives off infrared radiation (heat). Greenhouse gases, such as water vapour, carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄) and nitrous oxide (N₂O), absorb some of this heat and send part of it back down, keeping the planet warmer than it would otherwise be.

This natural greenhouse effect is essential: without it, the Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18 °C instead of about 15 °C, and most life could not exist. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect: human activities have added extra greenhouse gases, trapping more heat.

body.tip: Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get. Keep the two ideas separate when reading news stories.

list: Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas) for electricity, transport and industry releases CO₂; it is the largest cause.
Deforestation removes trees that absorb CO₂ and releases carbon stored in wood and soil.
Agriculture releases methane from livestock and rice paddies, and nitrous oxide from fertilisers.
Waste in landfills produces methane as it rots.
Some industrial processes, such as cement making, also release CO₂.

body.p: Before the industrial era, the atmosphere held about 280 parts per million (ppm) of CO₂. Measurements now show over 420 ppm, an increase of about (420 - 280) / 280 = 50%. Ice cores show this level is higher than at any time in at least 800 000 years.
Methane traps much more heat per molecule than CO₂ but stays in the air for only about a decade, so cutting methane slows warming quickly. CO₂ lasts for centuries, so its effects build up.

body.tip: Natural factors (the Sun, volcanoes, ocean cycles) affect climate too, but they cannot explain the rapid warming since the mid-twentieth century.

list: Global average surface temperature has risen by over 1 °C since the late 1800s, and recent years have been the warmest on record.
Oceans have absorbed most of the extra heat and about a quarter of the extra CO₂, making seawater more acidic and harming corals and shellfish.
Glaciers are shrinking worldwide, including on Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya, and Arctic sea ice is declining.
Sea level is rising as water warms and expands and as ice on land melts. At a rate of about 3.7 mm a year, that is about 11 cm in 30 years, and the rate is increasing.
Heatwaves, heavy rainfall events and some droughts are becoming more frequent or intense.

body.p: Evidence comes from thermometers on land and at sea, weather balloons, satellites, ocean floats, ice cores and tree rings. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) assesses thousands of studies and has concluded that it is unequivocal that human influence has warmed the atmosphere, ocean and land.

body.tip: Look for long-term trends in data, not single years; climate is about averages over decades.

body.p: Africa contributes only a small share of global greenhouse emissions, yet it is among the most vulnerable regions, because many people depend on rain-fed farming and there are fewer resources to adapt.

list: Farming and food: changing rainfall, droughts and heat reduce yields of crops such as maize; livestock suffer from heat and lack of pasture.
Water: droughts strain supplies for drinking, farming and hydropower, while floods damage homes and infrastructure.
Health: heat stress, and diseases such as malaria spreading to higher, previously cooler areas; floods raise the risk of cholera.
Coasts: rising seas and storm surges threaten cities such as Lagos, Dar es Salaam, Maputo and Alexandria.
Ecosystems: coral bleaching, shifting habitats and pressure on wildlife.
Conflict and migration: scarcity of land and water can increase tension and displacement.

body.p: Impacts fall hardest on the poor, women, children and the elderly, which is why climate justice, fairness in who bears costs and who pays for solutions, is central to international negotiations.

body.tip: Ask local elders how rains and seasons have changed in their lifetime; their observations often match the scientific record.

body.p: Mitigation means reducing greenhouse emissions or removing CO₂ from the air. Under the Paris Agreement, countries aim to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. Every fraction of a degree matters: the 0.5 °C difference between 1.5 °C and 2 °C means much worse heat extremes, crop losses and coral reef loss.

Because CO₂ builds up, there is a limited total amount, the carbon budget, that can be emitted for a given temperature limit. As an illustration, if a remaining budget were 400 billion tonnes of CO₂ and the world emitted 40 billion tonnes a year, it would be used up in 400 / 40 = 10 years. This is why emissions need to fall steeply, reaching net zero around mid-century.

list: Renewable energy: solar, wind, hydro and geothermal; Africa has some of the best solar resources in the world.
Energy efficiency: LED lighting, efficient appliances and better buildings.
Clean transport: public transport, walking and cycling, and electric vehicles.
Protecting and restoring forests, and better farming practices.
Clean cooking: replacing charcoal and firewood with cleaner stoves and fuels.

body.p: A household using 100 kWh of grid electricity a month, where each kWh produces about 0.9 kg of CO₂, emits 90 kg a month or 1080 kg a year. Rooftop solar covering 60% of that use would avoid about 648 kg of CO₂ a year.

body.tip: Calculate your own electricity emissions from your bill and your grid's emission factor.

body.p: Adaptation means adjusting to current and expected climate change to reduce harm. Because some warming is already locked in, adaptation is essential alongside mitigation.

list: Climate-smart agriculture: drought-tolerant crop varieties, conservation farming, agroforestry and better weather and seasonal forecasts for farmers.
Water: rainwater harvesting, efficient irrigation and protecting catchments and wetlands.
Early warning systems for floods, storms and heatwaves, which save lives.
Resilient infrastructure: drainage, flood defences and buildings designed for heat.
Restoring mangroves and wetlands, which buffer coasts from storms.
Insurance and social protection to help families recover after disasters.

body.p: Save energy and water, plant and protect trees, reduce waste, choose low-carbon transport when possible, and talk about climate change with family and community. Small actions add up: replacing eight 40 W bulbs with 10 W LED bulbs saves 8 x 30 W = 240 W. Used 4 hours a day, that is 0.24 x 4 x 365 = 350.4 kWh a year, avoiding about 315 kg of CO₂ on a grid emitting 0.9 kg per kWh.

Young people across Africa are leading climate action, from tree-planting drives to campaigns and green start-ups. Careers in renewable energy, environmental science, climate finance and sustainable agriculture are growing.

body.tip: Combine mitigation and adaptation: a solar-powered irrigation pump cuts emissions and makes farming more resilient to drought.

options: Stays in the air for only about a decade

options: A body that assesses climate science

quiz.q: Why is Africa especially vulnerable to climate change?
options: Many people rely on rain-fed farming and resources for adaptation are limited
It emits the most greenhouse gases
It is far from the sea
